title: Patience (III.3)
hookLine: the pharmacy line hasn't moved in six minutes; Francis de Sales wrote his chapter on patience for exactly this line
tomorrow: someone says great job. why is "it was nothing" the wrong answer?
last: FIT THE VIRTUE TO THE LIFE.

cards: The pharmacy line hasn't moved in six minutes. The person at the counter has a question, then another, then a coupon. You're already late.
Nobody would call this a great trial. Francis de Sales wrote for this line anyway. Yesterday he promised some virtues every life needs, and this is the first one he opens.

teach.b: Start with a line from Luke, in the Douay-Rheims: "In your patience you shall possess your souls." Patience, there, is how a person keeps hold of themselves. Notice the verb: possess.
Impatience quietly hands your soul over to the line, the coupon, the person at the counter. Patience keeps it. Next, the catch Francis spots.
People often accept a trial on their own terms: they'd bear it, if only it came without this inconvenience, or this embarrassment, or this person involved.
Real patience, he says, takes the trial God allows as it actually arrives.
Then, the small ones. The delay, the interruption, the little misunderstanding: they come often, so they're a steady place to practice. Last, the complaint.

teach.h: TELL THE ONE WHO CAN HELP.
teach.b: Complain little, he counsels, and when you need to tell someone, tell the person who can actually help.
So the shared virtues don't begin in a storm. They begin in a queue, and humility and gentleness come next.

how: Catholics count patience among the fruits of the Holy Spirit and often bring small daily impatience to prayer or to confession; Francis's chapter is a common reading on it.

o: waiting quietly until you finally get your way
bearing the trial that comes, as it comes, calmly
never letting anyone see that you are upset

games.q: patience, Francis's way — tap the pairs.
p: in your patience, possess your souls
only if it came without this or that
tell the one who can help

s: for Francis, patience means never telling anyone about your trouble
complain little, and when you need to, tell the person who can actually help.
he treats small daily irritations as real chances to practice
the delay, the interruption, the little misunderstanding.
patience means accepting a trial only once it fits your terms
that's the catch he names. real patience takes the trial as it arrives.

games.q: your friend's flight is delayed four hours. "i'd be fine," she texts, "if it weren't for the screaming toddler next to me." what would Francis's patience say?
o: take this delay as it came, toddler included.
patience is for big trials; a delay doesn't count.
complain loudly to everyone nearby until it changes.
games.why: Francis warns against bearing a trial only on your own terms; patience takes it as it actually comes, and the small ones count.

practice: Pick one sound that keeps going around you: traffic, a fan, the hum of a fridge. Stay with it through the sit without wishing it gone. When impatience rises, notice it, and come back to the sound.

wordCard.voice: Patience. Taking the trial that comes as it comes, big or small, and keeping hold of yourself in it.

orig.note: Latin: patience, as in the Vulgate's Luke 21:19, in patientia vestra.

carryVoice: Hold on to this: patience, the way to keep your soul in a line that won't move. That's the week.
